newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian coffee seen tight, stocks dwindle.
newsitem.headline: Colombian coffee seen tight, stocks dwindle.

text.p: Colombian coffee supplies will remain tight until the main harvest in October and world prices for arabicas seem likely to remain firm despite recent setbacks, a senior member of the National Coffee Federation said this week.
Federation commercial manager John Naranjo said output between now and the end of the 1996/97 year will "be very low" but added that inventories currently stood at about 4 million 60- kg bags.

Calculations based on the federation's own figures of actual crop and estimates for the remainder of the year show total output is set to be no higher than 9.7 million bags, compared to the federation's latest official forecast of "about 10 million bags".

Earlier this week Merrill Lynch issued a report in New York reflecting worries about supplies of top-quality coffees to international markets and concurred with calculations that second-largest grower Colombia's harvest was set to come in around 9.7 million bags "at best case scenario".
"If there's a slight recovery in availability it will be toward the end of the year because between now and October output will be very low," Naranjo told Reuters.
"I don't think that anybody really knows what the price level is going to do...with the limited offer of arabicas for the next few months I believe prices will remain firm," he added.
The federation has already said it will draw extensively on stocks to meet export schedules but has admitted much of these are not fresh crop.

Federation chiefs have still not issued a detailed breakdown on the precise quality of inventories but said they would be "using all technological means possible" to clean beans affected by the berry-borer or "broca" -- a quality not usually exported.
Private exporters believe much of the 4 million bags stocks that Naranjo referred to were beans from harvests between 1995 and 1991.

Earlier this week the federation released figures showing the May harvest was 836,000 60-kg bags, up 12.21 percent from the 745,000 bags produced in the same month last year. The total for the first two months of the April/June quarter to 1.66 million bags.
But the federation's estimate for the current quarter is for 3 million bags.

Taking into account that the October/December quarter came in at 3.6 million 60-kg bags and output in the January/March quarter was 1.94 million bags, the total 1996/97 crop would still only be 9.7 million bags even if the June forecast meets the 1 million bag target along with the 1.5 million bags estimated for July to September.
Allowing for domestic consumption of about 1.5 million bags, only 8.2 million bags would be available for export compared to export commitments of some 11 million bags.
The lowest official estimate the federation has given for the 1996/97 coffee year harvest so far is "about 10 million bags".
In its report Merill Lynch indicated Colombia's 1996/97 coffee crop would fall below federation estimates, saying: "At best case scenario production might be 9.7 million bags.
"Deliverable supplies should remain exceptionally tight through the September expiration and in advance of the peak consumption period," the report added.
Coffee on the New York exchange, however, continued its slide, heading to a six-week low at the close at 207.65 U.S. cents for July delivery, compared to a 20-year high of 318 cents on May 29.
